text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Respectful, trauma-informed shared decisions: take her account of her symptoms seriously, explain each medicine and its reason plainly, write the plan down, and check costs with her before prescribing
  • Cardiology consultation on the day of the two-week visit, with an echocardiogram, to find the cause of the breathlessness, review the antiplatelet choice and the other medicines, and advise on rehabilitation and a return to the stage
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy, aspirin 81 mg with a P2Y12 inhibitor, for twelve months from the heart attack, never stopped without speaking to cardiology; then aspirin alone
  • Atorvastatin 80 mg daily; lipid panel four to eight weeks after the start; goal LDL below 70 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall; lipoprotein(a) measured once
  • Metoprolol succinate for at least the first year after the heart attack; lisinopril for high blood pressure, with home readings and a target below 130/80 mmHg; potassium and creatinine one to two weeks after any dose change
  • Enroll in a 36-session outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program, starting within two weeks, with exercise training, nutrition, stress management and psychological support; the clinic will call her if she misses sessions
  • Depression after a heart attack: PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 today, repeat PHQ-9 at about twelve weeks, the rehabilitation program's psychologist, and a lower threshold for treatment if symptoms rise
  • Chest-pain action plan: nitroglycerin under the tongue, and 911 if pain is not better five minutes after the first tablet; warning symptoms in women, such as breathlessness, unusual tiredness, nausea or jaw, back or arm discomfort, explained
  • Costs: generic medicines in 90-day fills, the clinic social worker for debt advice and help with medicine costs, and rehabilitation sessions at times that fit her family
  • Women's cardiovascular risk: record the hysterectomy of her thirties and a possible early menopause as a risk-enhancing factor; hormone therapy is not used to prevent heart disease
  • Change ticagrelor to clopidogrel for ticagrelor-related breathlessness: 600 mg loading dose 24 hours after the last ticagrelor, then 75 mg daily, without a gap in antiplatelet cover
  • Raise lisinopril to 10 mg daily for blood pressure above target, with potassium and creatinine one to two weeks later
  • Laboratory tests drawn at the rehabilitation center on session days, so that no check needs a separate trip
  • Nosebleed plan on dual antiplatelet therapy: firm pressure on the soft part of the nose for 15 minutes, saline spray and a humidifier; do not stop aspirin or clopidogrel; come in if bleeding lasts more than 30 minutes
  • Graded return to the stage: rehearsals at the effort reached in rehabilitation, then full performances, with rest between shows, water, and nitroglycerin in the dressing room

resource.title: Josephine Baker synthetic care plan
resource.description: Secondary prevention in the first months after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction in a 62-year-old Black woman, an entertainer, veteran and civil rights activist under heavy financial strain, seen three weeks after a stent with breathlessness on exertion. The episode covers the care women, and Black women in particular, are less likely to receive after a heart attack, as AHA statements and registry data show: a full cardiology review, echocardiography, cardiac rehabilitation and every guideline-directed medicine. It teaches dual antiplatelet therapy for twelve months, recognizing ticagrelor-related breathlessness and switching to clopidogrel with a loading dose rather than stopping; high-intensity atorvastatin with an LDL goal below 70 mg/dL and a single lipoprotein(a) measurement; a beta-blocker for the first year and an ACE inhibitor for high blood pressure, with potassium and kidney checks (one missed check recorded honestly); depression screening after a heart attack with the PHQ-2 and PHQ-9, as the AHA advises; a nosebleed on dual antiplatelet therapy managed without stopping it; a graded return to the stage after an exercise test; the hysterectomy of her thirties as a possible early menopause and a risk-enhancing factor; and trauma-informed, respectful care that takes her account of her body seriously, under the 1966 AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, the 1968 ACC/AHA acute coronary syndromes guideline and the AHA statement on myocardial infarction in women.
